case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by foster children either directly or through 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
key_cases.relevance: Audit and fiscal findings under the same IV-E framework are enforced through funding penalties rather than litigation.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

key_cases.case_name: Pontarelli v. Rhode Island Department of Elementary & Secondary Education
key_cases.holding: The requested records fell within an APRA exception and were not public records, so the agency's denial was upheld; separately, any reason not stated in the denial is deemed waived absent good cause.
key_cases.relevance: Audit-adjacent personnel and investigative material held by a state agency may fall outside APRA entirely.
key_cases.quote: we hold without hesitation that the records Pontarelli requested are not public records for the purposes of APRA

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: A section 1983 plaintiff must identify the particular statutory provision said to confer an individual federal right; Title IV-D's 'substantial compliance' requirement is only a systemwide yardstick for the Secretary and confers no such right, so the judgment was vacated for provision-by-provision analysis.
key_cases.relevance: Blessing describes the funding-reduction mechanism as the enforcement tool for plan noncompliance, which is the same fiscal-penalty track that governs IV-E audit findings against Rhode Island.
key_cases.quote: In order to seek redress through § 1983, however, a plaintiff must assert the violation of a federal right, not merely a violation of federal law.

key_cases.case_name: Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Spending Clause statutes can create rights enforceable under section 1983; the Federal Nursing Home Reform Act's unnecessary-restraint and predischarge-notice provisions unambiguously confer individual rights, and the Act's own enforcement scheme does not foreclose a section 1983 suit, so the judgment for the resident was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Talevski leaves fiscal and audit conditions enforced through funding penalties while preserving private enforcement for provisions that are genuinely rights-creating.
key_cases.quote: our precedent sets a demanding bar: Statutory provisions must unambiguously confer individual federal rights.
